newsitem.title: USA: Ohio governor emphasizes schools in speech.
newsitem.headline: Ohio governor emphasizes schools in speech.

text.p: Ohio Gov. George Voinovich made it clear in his state of the state address Tuesday that schools will be a top priority in the state's upcoming biennial budget.
Calling education Ohio's "number one priority," Voinovich outlined several initiatives already underway to improve schools.
Voinovich's speech did not directly address an impending ruling by the Ohio Supreme Court on the constitutionality of the state's current system of funding schools.

A Perry County court judge in 1994 found the system to be unconstitutional because it resulted in wide disparities between wealthy and poor districts. That ruling was overturned by a state appellate court in 1995.
Still, Voinovich said the new fiscal 1998-99 budget would include $213 million towards balancing funding inequities between poor and wealthy school districts.

He also proposed $300 million in state support for school buildings, with $200 million of that amount targeted to the 60 lowest property wealth districts in the state and $100 million for the state's eight largest urban districts.
Voinovich said the budget would also recommend using $30 million in excess lottery funds to fix electrical problems at schools to bring computers into classrooms.
A summary of school funding initiatives from the governor's office also indicated that the upcoming budget would guarentee annual state per-pupil funding of $3,767 by 1999.
Voinovich is expected to unveil his two-year budget plan as early as next month.
The governor also called for the development of performance audits for schools. He praised a school choice program underway in Cleveland, and proposed a pilot charter school program in Lucas County.
On the tax front, Voinovich asked lawmakers to maintain a two-year income tax cut they passed last year by making a income tax reduction fund permanent.
Voinovich also reported that the state's rainy day fund now stands at $828 million, representing a reserve of five percent. He said the fund was at a "responsible" level that should not be changed.
He also pointed out that the fund, as well as the state's fiscal conservatism led to upgrades in the state's general obligation bond rating last year.
